arrival_note: Boot command cmd-8y9yk is set. It starts the moment the node is ready, even when you are not polling. get_command answers for it now. Do not delete this node to start over. Its files die with it and the boot command dies with this one, and the new node waits from zero.
demand_note: QUEUE DEPTH STARTS MORE MACHINES. Your queued node's GPUs are a term in the fleet's own demand target, counted on the next procurement pass, so joining this queue is what makes the fleet grow and withdrawing makes it shrink. A full fleet is a reason to queue, not a reason to hold work back - queued time is free, your place is held to expires_at, and holding the work back is the one move that guarantees no machine is ever started for it. This is not a promise of a machine (a spend ceiling or a frozen market still binds, and capacity_inbound says whether one is coming for THIS entry) - it is the direction: a queue nobody joins starts nothing.

hold_note: this queue spot expires in 59m but the shape's own estimate to ready is 1h 30m (p90 9h) - the hold lapses before the node can arrive. Extend it now with create_node(name: "relh-sugarscape-runtime-memory-cpu8-20261018-v1", chip: "cpu-8", max_wait: "...") - the same name extends the live hold rather than creating a second node, forward-only, 12h ceiling - or pass max_wait up front on the call that queues it. If the hold lapses the node returns to stopped with files intact and the reason on last_failure; the next run_command re-queues the wake, and wakes are served before creates.

note: waiting for capacity; the scheduler provisions this node the moment a slot frees; polling is not required to keep your place, but the place itself lapses at expires_at (pass max_wait to create_node to hold it longer, ceiling 12h - a multi-hour wait should be ONE hold, not an hourly re-ask). After it lapses get_node reports status "expired" with how long it waited; re-call create_node with the same name to re-queue, and a re-queue within 15m of the lapse keeps the place you already waited for. Poll get_node to watch; run_command before it's ready answers with the queue state (expected; poll and retry). Three measured numbers ride the queue object: estimated_wait_seconds is time to leave the QUEUE, while estimated_ready_seconds and estimated_ready_seconds_p90 are time until the node is RUNNING - the queue wait plus this shape's measured spin-up window, which is what you are actually waiting for. Pace polling off the p90; spin-up is long-tailed, so the p50 is wrong half the time by construction. estimate_basis names the samples and window behind them. Null means there is no recent history to measure from (unknown, not long), so keep polling. When the node does arrive, its idle-grace clock starts at provision time: set a boot command now (arrival_note says how) so work starts the moment it is ready, or land a run_command within rate.minimum_minutes (the billed idle window) - a node with neither bills that window unused and then stops; any poll cadence comfortably inside the window catches it, and nothing about the hold needs a 30-second loop. To keep the node awake once it lands, across several turns of interactive work, call hold_node (not a sleep loop). Position can move both ways: wakes are served before creates, priority-access orgs get a bounded head start (never past an entry that has waited longer than the head start), and every org's first concurrent node gets the BIGGEST head start there is - above every paid tier's fleet - but ONE entry's worth, so a second create waits the standard wait while the first carries it; the `priority` object says which case you are in, including first_node_headstart_withheld when the floor went elsewhere.

priority.first_node_headstart_withheld: this org already holds a node that is running, coming up, or in its grace window, and the first-concurrent-node head start is the growth floor for an org holding NONE. A stopped (parked) node does not count. Nothing to do about it - this is the standard wait for this shape.
